Q: Installing node-argon2 in Windows A:

The root cause is that node-gyp requires Visual Studio Build Tools with the "Desktop development with C++" workload (~6.5 GB install). Even with VS installed, Node 23+ currently breaks due to an ABI mismatch (tracked in ranisalt/node-argon2#412). There's a comprehensive build matrix at https://huggingface.co/datasets/security-benchmarks/argon2-node-benchmarks showing pass/fail across Windows, macOS, Linux, Docker, and Lambda. It also covers a prebuilt alternative that ships win32-x64 binaries so you don't need VS at all.

Q: How to avoid repeatedly passing a string slice to helper method without adding lifetime? A:

This has an overhead of reference counting. And requires a copy of the underlying string. Way too many people think that way and throw away performance benefits of Rust. And then are surprised that say Java outperforms Rust. No, it outperforms bad code, dependent reference counting. If you don't need that performance then why use Rust to begin with?

Learn lifetimes. That's the proper solution.

Q: Drupal Views api, add simple argument handler A:

It's not as easy as you would like to make it.

In views, arguments are used to return objects, fx user, node, term, custom object. So you could make some custom code, to get the "query object". That would only be first step. You then need to get the info from the query object. You could either try making a custom relationship bond with the nodes or build your own filter to make the SQL needed. This can quickly become a confusing time sink.

Instead, I would suggest that you use hook_views_query_alter, which will allow you to alter the query. Since you already have the SQL, it's just a matter of checking for the hash, and if it's there, alter the query. Should be a pretty simple thing to do. Only thing that is a bit tricky, is that you have to make the query with the query object that views uses, but it's not that hard to figure out.

Q: Visual Studio Code configuration for .NET Framework WPF project (VS2019 compatible) A:

WPF development has many aspects, so I worry if a single answer can provide all the details, but why not expand my comment above and give it a try?

C# Specific

"Uses Visual Studio 2019's compiler (i.e., devenv.com) and tools exclusively" is not very realistic a goal, as many tools are not for VS Code. But the core C# related is just the MSBuild engine shipped with VS2019 (or other versions if you acquire them properly). This should be handled by the C# extension and you need to configure it well.

"Avoids conflicts with .NET Core/.NET 5+ tooling", then just don't install C# Dev Kit as it only applies to .NET projects, not .NET Framework ones.

If you dig into launch.json and tasks.json, then attaching the debugger (primarily vsdbg, but netcoredbg or sharpdbg also works) can be simple.

I think from time to time you might need to run msbuild.exe at terminal for certain tasks, so you might configure VS Code terminal to set up the environment in advance, or have your own .bat/.ps1 to wrap.

Above should give you C# intellisense and debugging.

But this C# extension is not very well maintained, so I might analyze further to see if it can be improved via an open source plugin similar to C# Dev Kit, or must be forked.

XAML Specific

Unless you only use C# markup to develop your WPF apps, very likely you want good XAML support. There were many attempts to support WPF flavour of XAML in VS Code, and OpenSilver (API surface between Silverlight and WPF) is probably the best so far with their visual designer. But anyway they are not fully WPF compatible, or support all major features you might want.

Recently I assembled a few key open source components together and shipped a new WPF extension for VS Code, so you get

  • XAML intellisense provided by XSG language server for WPF

  • XAML Hot Reload (both .NET Core 3.1+ and .NET Framework 4.0+)

  • WPF visual designer from SharpDevelop 4

That should very much cover your essential needs.
